title: Taking Sides Amid the Storm: Musk Backs Jensen Huang with a Single 'I Agree'

content_html:
On November 9, Tesla CEO Elon Musk reposted a post on X about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, adding just two words: "I agree." The seemingly casual statement was backed by a personal controversy sweeping Silicon Valley—earlier the same day, IT Home reported that Jensen Huang had sent an apology letter to Nvidia employees, admitting to an extramarital affair and saying he hoped to regain the trust of his family and colleagues. When the head of an AI chip giant becomes embroiled in a personal conduct controversy, Musk, the most influential voice among his peers, chose to publicly support him—a strong signal indeed.

What Musk reposted were five comments on Jensen Huang from Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire, whose wording swung back and forth between criticism and defense: he called Huang "one of the most outstanding entrepreneurs of this generation," then immediately added that "he did something extremely stupid," and said bluntly that "this is bad for America"; but Maguire also speculated that Huang "did not mean any harm," and pointed out that "making two mistakes does not mean the mistakes can be rationalized." After going in circles, he landed on the most important line—Huang's leadership in the U.S. AI industry is "indispensable." Musk's "I agree" endorsed precisely that final point.

This controversy reflects a reality of the AI era: top operators are hard to replace. With GPUs and its compute ecosystem, Nvidia has a chokehold on global AI infrastructure, and Jensen Huang's personal strategic judgment is so deeply tied to the company that capital markets and industry find it hard to completely separate the "person" from the "company."

The apology letter has been sent, and public opinion may continue to simmer, but the successive statements from Musk and Sequoia show that, with the AI race at a fever pitch, the industry's reliance on this leader has by no means been easily shaken by a personal conduct controversy.
